wine.name: Krug Grande Cuvée
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir, Chardonnay and Meunier, in proportions that change with each Édition.
wine.sites: Plots across the villages of Champagne, each kept apart as its own wine, and a library of reserve wines from many years.
wine.making: Each plot is fermented on its own in small, old oak casks that let the wine breathe without giving it any taste of wood. At least a hundred and twenty wines from more than ten years are blended, reserve wines among them, and the bottles rest at least seven years on their lees in the Reims cellars.
wine.glass: Toasted brioche, roasted hazelnut and candied lemon peel over ripe pear and honeyed pastry, with a fine, persistent mousse, a broad, almost vinous weight and a long, dry, faintly smoky finish.
wine.ageing: Drinks well on release and keeps developing for a decade or two after it, gaining toffee, coffee and dried fig.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius, never ice cold; no need to decant; a wide white wine glass shows it better than a narrow flute.

label.means: The release's place in the line of yearly blends; each Édition is built around one harvest.
A code on the back label that opens, on the house's site, the story of that bottle.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre after disgorging.

records.table: Krug Grande Cuvée is the house's whole idea in one bottle: more than a hundred and twenty wines from over ten years, fermented in small old casks and aged at least seven years. It drinks like a mature white Burgundy with bubbles, so pour it in a wine glass.
records.story: Joseph Krug (1800 to 1866), born in Mainz, learned Champagne at the house of Jacquesson before founding his own in Reims in 1843. In 1848 he set down his creed in a personal notebook: to make, every year and whatever the weather, the fullest expression of Champagne by blending the wines of many plots and many years. For more than a century that blend was sold as Private Cuvée, and in 1978 the house renamed it Grande Cuvée. The family added a vintage, a rosé and, from the walled Clos du Mesnil, a Chardonnay of one vineyard first made from the 1979 vintage, but the blend remained the house's purpose. Krug kept fermenting in small oak casks while most houses turned to steel tanks, and it built a library of reserve wines from many years for the cellar master to draw on. In 2016 the house began to give each release an Édition number, so that a guest can tell one year's Grande Cuvée from the next and read the harvest it was built around. A sommelier sells it as a wine to be tasted, not a toast to be drunk.

others.name: Krug Vintage
others.note: Declared years only, made with the same small casks and long cellar ageing as the Grande Cuvée.

others.name: Krug Clos du Mesnil
others.note: Chardonnay alone from one walled vineyard in Le Mesnil-sur-Oger, first made from the 1979 vintage.

others.name: Krug Clos d'Ambonnay
others.note: The Pinot Noir counterpart from a tiny walled plot in Ambonnay, first made in 1995.

traps: Grande Cuvée carries no vintage, yet it spends longer in the cellar than many vintage Champagnes.
Clos du Mesnil is Chardonnay from Le Mesnil-sur-Oger; Clos d'Ambonnay is Pinot Noir from Ambonnay.
An Édition number counts the yearly creations of the blend; it is not a vintage year.

cards.front: Krug Grande Cuvée: what is fermented in small old oak casks, and why?
cards.back: Every plot's wine, kept apart; the old casks let the wine breathe without adding any taste of wood.

cards.front: What does the Édition number on Krug Grande Cuvée tell a guest?
cards.back: Which yearly creation of the blend it is, numbered since 2016; each is built around one harvest with reserve wines from many years.

questions.q: A guest notices that Krug Grande Cuvée carries no vintage on its label. Which explanation is right?
opts: It blends over a hundred wines from more than ten years
It is a single vintage held back for seven years
It comes only from the walled Clos du Mesnil
It is a Blanc de Blancs from the Côte des Blancs
questions.exp: Grande Cuvée is a multi vintage blend of well over a hundred wines, reserve wines among them; a single vintage would carry its year, and Clos du Mesnil is a separate Chardonnay.

questions.q: Joseph Krug learned his trade at Jacquesson. In which city did he found his own house in 1843?
opts: Reims
Épernay
Aÿ
Châlons-sur-Marne
questions.exp: Krug was founded in Reims in 1843; Jacquesson was then at Châlons-sur-Marne, and Épernay and Aÿ are the towns of other houses.

report: One account dates the Private Cuvée label from 1862; with no second source the story says only that it was sold under that name for more than a century before 1978.
The purchase year of Clos du Mesnil is left out for want of a second source; the library's first vintage of 1979 is used.

wine.name: Dom Pérignon
wine.grapes: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, in close to equal parts that shift with the year.
wine.sites: Chiefly Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs and the Montagne de Reims, with Hautvillers, the abbey's own village.
wine.making: Made only in declared vintages, from base wines fermented in steel tanks with no oak, then aged on the lees for the better part of a decade before the first release. The same vintage returns later as Plénitude 2, after some fifteen years on its lees.
wine.glass: Toasted almond, white peach and fresh brioche, with a smoky note of struck flint and a fine, creamy mousse; with age it moves towards roasted coffee, candied ginger and acacia honey.
wine.ageing: Approachable on release, it gains depth for fifteen to twenty years and more, which is why the house releases each vintage again as Plénitudes.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass rather than a narrow flute.

label.means: Dom Pérignon is always the wine of one year, and the label prints it.
The same vintage released again after about fifteen years on its lees, often written P2.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre after disgorging.

records.table: Dom Pérignon is Moët & Chandon's prestige cuvée, named for the Benedictine monk who kept the cellars of Hautvillers. It is always a single vintage of Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, aged for years on its lees before release.
records.story: Claude Moët (1683 to 1760) founded his wine house at Épernay in 1743, and his grandson Jean-Rémy Moët (1758 to 1841) carried its wines across Europe and counted the Emperor Napoleon among his customers. In 1833 a son-in-law of the Chandon family became a partner and the house took the name Moët & Chandon. Its prestige cuvée honours Dom Pierre Pérignon (1638 to 1715), cellarer of the Benedictine abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 until his death. He did not invent sparkling Champagne: he blended grapes from different villages, refined the pressing of black grapes for white juice and, like the winemakers of his day, tried to keep bubbles out of the wine. The name Dom Pérignon belonged to the house of Mercier, which passed it to Moët after a marriage between the two families in 1927. The first Dom Pérignon, from the 1921 vintage, was released in 1936. It has since been made only in declared years, and the house releases the same vintage a second and a third time, as Plénitudes, after far longer ageing on the lees.

others.name: Moët Impérial
others.note: The house's non vintage Brut of Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay, its everyday style.

others.name: Moët & Chandon Grand Vintage
others.note: The vintage wine under the Moët name, made apart from Dom Pérignon.

others.name: Dom Pérignon Rosé
others.note: The rosé of a declared year, made in far smaller quantity.

traps: Dom Pérignon did not invent sparkling Champagne: he blended villages, pressed black grapes for white juice and tried to avoid bubbles.
Dom Pérignon is always vintage dated; Moët Impérial is the house's non vintage Brut.
Plénitude 2 is not a different blend: it is the same vintage disgorged after a far longer stay on its lees.

cards.front: Who was Dom Pierre Pérignon, and what did he truly do?
cards.back: Cellarer of the abbey of Hautvillers from 1668 to his death in 1715; he refined blending and the pressing of black grapes for white wine, but did not invent the bubbles.

cards.front: Moët & Chandon's Dom Pérignon: which grapes, and is there a non vintage version?
cards.back: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in close to equal parts; it is always the wine of a single declared year.

questions.q: A guest ordering Dom Pérignon asks which grapes go into it. What do you tell them?
opts: Chardonnay and Pinot Noir, in close to equal parts
Chardonnay alone, as a Blanc de Blancs
Pinot Noir, Meunier and Chardonnay together
Pinot Noir alone, as a Blanc de Noirs
questions.exp: Dom Pérignon blends Chardonnay and Pinot Noir in close to equal parts in each declared year; Meunier goes into Moët Impérial, the house's non vintage Brut.

questions.q: How did the name Dom Pérignon come to Moët & Chandon before the first release of 1936?
opts: The house of Mercier passed it on after a family marriage
The abbey of Hautvillers sold it at auction
Napoleon granted it to the Moët family in 1804
The Comité Champagne assigned it to the largest house
questions.exp: The name was an unused mark of the house of Mercier, given to Moët after a Mercier married a Chandon in 1927; the 1921 vintage was the first released.

report: Dom Pérignon is presented today apart from Moët's other wines; the record keeps to history, Moët's prestige cuvée since 1936, and says nothing that will age.
The count of bottles or cases of the first release differs between accounts and is left out.
The year the Chandon partner joined is 1833 in most accounts and 1832 in one.

wine.name: Cristal
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir and Chardonnay, the Pinot Noir usually the larger part, about three parts to two.
wine.sites: Only the house's own Grand Cru vineyards, chiefly in the Montagne de Reims and the Côte des Blancs; no bought grapes.
wine.making: Made only in years the house judges ripe enough, from estate parcels vinified apart, a share of them in large oak tuns, with the malolactic conversion usually avoided to keep its tension. It rests about six years on its lees and at least eight months more after disgorging.
wine.glass: Meyer lemon, white peach and fresh almond over crushed chalk, with a delicate, creamy mousse; time brings toasted brioche, hazelnut and honeyed pastry while the line stays taut and saline.
wine.ageing: Taut on release, it opens after eight to ten years and keeps for twenty or more in a cool cellar.
wine.serve: 8 to 10 degrees Celsius; no need to decant; a tulip or a white wine glass, the cellophane left on until the bottle is opened.

label.means: The cuvée's name, from the clear glass of the first bottles made for the Tsar.
The house that makes it; Cristal is its prestige cuvée, not a separate producer.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre after disgorging.

records.table: Cristal is Louis Roederer's prestige cuvée, first made in 1876 for Tsar Alexander II in the clear bottle he asked for. It comes only from the house's own Grand Cru vines, mostly Pinot Noir, and only in years ripe enough.
records.story: The house that became Louis Roederer was a Reims wine business recorded in 1776. A nephew of its owner inherited it in 1833 and gave it his own name, Louis Roederer, and under him and his son the house sold widely in Russia. In 1876 Tsar Alexander II (1818 to 1881) asked the house to set aside its prestige cuvée for his court each year, and it was bottled in clear glass with a flat base so that, as the story is told, nothing could be hidden in the bottle or its punt. The wine took its name, Cristal, from that glass. The revolution of 1917 took from the house its first customer and much of its Russian trade, and Cristal later became a wine any guest could order; a rosé followed in 1974. Unlike most houses, Roederer built its prestige wine on its own vineyards rather than on bought grapes, and Cristal is still made only in the years the house judges ripe enough. The coloured cellophane round each bottle is there to keep light from a wine in clear glass.

others.name: Cristal Rosé
others.note: The rosé of a declared year, first made in 1974, in far smaller quantity.

others.name: Louis Roederer Collection
others.note: The house's numbered multi vintage Brut, which replaced Brut Premier.

others.name: Louis Roederer Blanc de Blancs
others.note: A vintage Chardonnay from the Côte des Blancs.

traps: Cristal is always vintage: there is no non vintage Cristal.
Cristal is Louis Roederer's cuvée from Reims, not the wine of Roederer Estate in California.
The clear bottle dates from the Tsar's order of 1876; the cellophane wrap is there to keep the light out.

cards.front: Louis Roederer Cristal: for whom was it first made, and when?
cards.back: For Tsar Alexander II of Russia, in 1876, in a clear glass bottle with a flat base.

cards.front: Where do the grapes for Cristal come from?
cards.back: Only from Louis Roederer's own Grand Cru vineyards, mostly Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, and only in declared years.

questions.q: A guest asks whether Cristal is a blend of bought grapes, like many prestige cuvées. What is true?
opts: It comes only from the house's own vineyards
It is a non vintage blend of bought grapes
It is made largely from bought Meunier
It is a single vineyard Blanc de Blancs
questions.exp: Cristal is drawn only from Louis Roederer's own Grand Cru vines, Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, in declared years; it is never non vintage and holds no Meunier.

questions.q: Why was the first Cristal of 1876 bottled in clear glass with a flat base?
opts: The Tsar wished to see that nothing was hidden in it
Clear glass let the cellar watch the second fermentation
Flat bases stood better on the decks of ships
French law of the time required clear bottles
questions.exp: As the house tells it, Tsar Alexander II wanted a bottle in which nothing could be hidden; the coloured cellophane of today simply keeps light off the clear glass.

The villages of Cristal's parcels were not confirmed; the record names the districts only.
The oak share and the malolactic choice vary by vintage in the house's own sheets; the record says a share and usually.

wine.name: La Grande Année
wine.grapes: Pinot Noir, about two thirds, with Chardonnay for the rest.
wine.sites: Some twenty crus, mostly Grand Cru, the Pinot Noir chiefly from Aÿ and Verzenay.
wine.making: Every base wine is fermented in old oak barrels. The wine is then aged under natural cork rather than a crown cap, for seven years and more on its lees, and every bottle is riddled and disgorged by hand.
wine.glass: Baked apple, ripe pear and roasted hazelnut over toasted brioche, with a savoury, almost mushroom depth from the Pinot Noir and the barrels, a firm, vinous body and a fine, steady mousse.
wine.ageing: Rich enough on release, it grows more savoury and nutty over ten to twenty years.
wine.serve: 9 to 11 degrees Celsius; no need to decant, though a few minutes in the glass help; a tulip or a white wine glass.

label.means: The great year: Bollinger's name for its vintage wine, made only in years the house declares.
The Grand Cru village where the house stands and grows much of its Pinot Noir.
Dry: less than twelve grams of sugar a litre after disgorging.

records.table: La Grande Année is Bollinger's vintage Champagne: Pinot Noir led, fermented entirely in oak barrels and aged under cork for years before it is disgorged by hand. It has the weight to stand beside a main course.
records.story: Bollinger was founded at Aÿ in 1829 by three partners, one of them a young German salesman whose name the house carries. It received a Royal Warrant from Queen Victoria in 1884, and British drinkers have followed it ever since. After her husband's death in 1941, Elisabeth Bollinger, known as Lily (1899 to 1977), ran the house through the German occupation and on until 1971. She cycled through the vineyards to inspect them, bought more vines and launched R.D., a vintage disgorged late after a long rest on its lees. The house kept old ways that others dropped: fermenting in old barrels, holding its reserve wines in magnum under cork and tending two small plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir inside Aÿ, the source of Vieilles Vignes Françaises. La Grande Année is the wine in which all of that shows: a vintage of Pinot Noir with Chardonnay, fermented in barrel, aged under cork and riddled by hand, from a house that has stayed in the founding family's line.

others.name: Bollinger Special Cuvée
others.note: The non vintage Brut, Pinot Noir led, its reserve wines kept in magnum.

others.name: Bollinger R.D.
others.note: La Grande Année held far longer on its lees and disgorged late; R.D. means recently disgorged.

others.name: Bollinger Vieilles Vignes Françaises
others.note: A Blanc de Noirs from two small plots of ungrafted Pinot Noir in Aÿ.

traps: R.D. is not a vineyard or a separate blend: it is La Grande Année disgorged years later.
Vieilles Vignes Françaises is ungrafted Pinot Noir, not old vine Chardonnay.
La Grande Année is fermented in oak, yet it is not meant to taste of new wood: the barrels are old.

cards.front: Bollinger La Grande Année: how is it fermented and aged?
cards.back: Entirely in old oak barrels, then aged under natural cork rather than a crown cap, and riddled and disgorged by hand.

cards.front: What does R.D. mean on a Bollinger label?
cards.back: Recently disgorged: La Grande Année left far longer on its lees and disgorged late, a style launched in Lily Bollinger's time.

questions.q: Which grape leads the blend of Bollinger La Grande Année, as it leads the house style?
opts: Pinot Noir
Chardonnay
Meunier
Pinot Blanc
questions.exp: Pinot Noir, about two thirds and largely from Aÿ and Verzenay, leads La Grande Année, with Chardonnay for the rest; Meunier plays no part in it.

questions.q: Who ran Bollinger from 1941 to 1971 and is remembered for inspecting the vineyards by bicycle?
opts: Lily Bollinger
Barbe-Nicole Clicquot
Louise Pommery
Camille Olry-Roederer
questions.exp: Elisabeth, known as Lily, Bollinger led the house after her husband's death in 1941; the widows Clicquot and Pommery ran their houses in the nineteenth century.

sources.title: Bollinger: La Grande Année, ten years of patience

report: The founders' first names differ between accounts (Athanase or Hennequin de Villermont, Joseph or Jacques Bollinger), so the story names none of them.
Lily Bollinger's years are given as 1899 to 1977; the refuter should confirm them in a second source.

wine.name: Substance
wine.grapes: Chardonnay alone: a Blanc de Blancs.
wine.sites: The domaine's own Grand Cru Chardonnay in Avize.
wine.making: Each year's wine, fermented in barrels with its own yeasts, is added to a solera begun in the mid 1980s and a part of the whole is drawn off to bottle, so every bottle carries a little of every year since. It is bottled with little dosage and long lees ageing, and the label gives the date of disgorging.
wine.glass: Bruised apple, walnut and salted caramel with a note of fino Sherry, over crushed chalk and lemon peel; dry, broad and vinous, with a fine mousse and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Ready on release, it gains nuttier, deeper notes for another decade, and many cellar it as they would white Burgundy.
wine.serve: 10 to 12 degrees Celsius, since colder it closes; decant it briefly if you like, or let it open in a white wine glass.

label.means: The grapes come from Avize, one of the seventeen Grand Cru villages of Champagne.
A white Champagne made from white grapes alone, here Chardonnay.
A grower making Champagne from its own grapes; printed as RM before the registration number.

records.table: Jacques Selosse is the Avize grower whose wines gave grower Champagne its name abroad, and Substance is its Chardonnay drawn from a solera, as in a Sherry bodega. It tastes of walnut, bruised apple and chalk: pour it in a wine glass, a little warmer than most Champagne.
records.story: Jacques Selosse is a small domaine in Avize, in the Côte des Blancs, whose family began bottling its own Champagne around 1960, by most accounts, rather than selling all its grapes to the houses. In 1980 the founder's son took charge. He had trained in Burgundy and brought its ways back to Champagne: low yields, ploughed soils, wild yeasts, fermentation in barrels and a wine made first as a wine of place and only then as a sparkling wine. In the mid 1980s, inspired by time spent in Jerez, he began a solera of Avize Chardonnay, in 1986 by most accounts: each year the new wine goes into the reserve and a part of the whole is drawn off to bottle, so the blend carries a little of every year since it began. That wine is Substance. Its oxidative, nutty depth divided drinkers, but it made Selosse the model for the grower movement of the 1990s and 2000s, when small estates across Champagne began to bottle their own wines and to name their villages and plots on the label.

others.name: Selosse Initial
others.note: The Grand Cru Blanc de Blancs that introduces the house style.

others.name: Selosse V.O. Version Originale
others.note: An Extra Brut Blanc de Blancs from the Grand Cru villages of the Côte des Blancs.

others.name: Selosse Lieux-dits
others.note: Single parcels bottled under their own names, the grower's clearest statement of place.

traps: Substance carries no vintage: it is drawn from a solera of many years.
Récoltant-Manipulant is a label code for a grower, not a mark of quality.
Its nutty, Sherry like notes come from age and air in the solera, not from any fortification.

cards.front: Jacques Selosse Substance: how is it made, and why does it carry no vintage?
cards.back: It is drawn from a solera of Avize Chardonnay begun in the mid 1980s: each year's wine is added and a part bottled, so every bottle blends many years.

cards.front: What did Jacques Selosse change in Champagne from 1980?
cards.back: It made Champagne as a wine of place, from low yields, wild yeasts and barrels, and gave the grower movement its model.

questions.q: A guest is surprised that Selosse Substance shows no vintage. Which method explains it?
opts: A solera, topped up each year with new wine
A blend of declared vintages from bought grapes
Saignée, bleeding juice from the Pinot Noir vats
Carbonation of a still Chardonnay before release
questions.exp: Substance is drawn from a solera of Avize Chardonnay begun in the mid 1980s; each year's wine refreshes it, so no single vintage applies. It uses no bought grapes and no saignée.

questions.q: Where did the heir who took charge of Jacques Selosse in 1980 train, before bringing barrel fermentation and low yields to Avize?
opts: Burgundy
Jerez
Bordeaux
Alsace
questions.exp: He trained in Burgundy and brought its handling of wine to Avize; Jerez inspired the solera of Substance later, in the mid 1980s.

sources.title: Vinous: Jacques Selosse, a study of Substance
Rare Wine Co: Selosse, out of the wilderness

report: The domaine's founding is 1949 in one account and the 1950s in others, so founded is left empty; first bottling around 1960 is in two accounts.
The solera's start is 1986 in most accounts and 1987 in one; the record says the mid 1980s and gives 1986 as most accounts have it.
Whether Substance comes from one parcel or two in Avize differs between accounts, so the record names the village only.
